cl_nic_smoking_health.q: How much does smoking shorten life?
cl_nic_smoking_health.short: About 11 to 12 years on average, a big US study estimates. Of 100 women who smoked, 38 would reach 80, against 70 who never smoked.
cl_nic_smoking_health.but: These are averages for groups in one US study, not a forecast for any one person. It looked at cigarettes only.
how: About 202,000 US adults aged 25 or older were interviewed in 1997 to 2004 and followed through death records for about 7 years. At ages 25 to 79, people who smoked died at about 3 times the rate of people who never smoked (under 100 cigarettes in their lives).

The gap was biggest for lung cancer, at about 15 to 18 times the rate, and other lung and breathing diseases, about 8 to 9 times. For heart disease it was about 3 times. The authors estimate that about 6 in 10 deaths among people who smoked at these ages wouldn't have happened at the disease death rates of people who never smoked.

Scaled to US death rates in 2004, 38 in 100 women and 26 in 100 men who smoked would live from 25 to 80, against 70 and 61 in 100 who never smoked. A 2014 US Surgeon General's report judges that smoking raises the risk of dying and causes disease in nearly every organ.

Compared with people who kept smoking, people who had stopped gained roughly 10 years if they stopped at 25 to 34, 9 at 35 to 44, 6 at 45 to 54 and 4 at 55 to 64. Those who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept on.
cl_nic_smoking_health.rate: One large nationwide study, linked to death records. It didn't account for diet, exercise or income, but those are unlikely to explain a threefold gap. The figures on stopping are rougher.

cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.q: Is it the nicotine or the smoke that does the harm?
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.short: Burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm, a big US report says. But it judges that nicotine on its own can still harm an unborn baby.
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.but: It doesn't say how much of smoking's harm comes from nicotine itself. And the report sums up other studies, so this is second-hand.
how: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report says burned tobacco, like cigarettes, causes by far most of tobacco's death and disease in the US. That's about products. It doesn't split the harm between nicotine and the rest of the smoke.

For nicotine alone, it found enough evidence that it can poison in high enough amounts. It also judged that nicotine harms an unborn baby's growing brain and adds to early births and stillbirths. The brain finding comes from lab studies, the pregnancy one mostly from smokeless tobacco and patch trials.

For teenagers' brains, it called the evidence suggestive but not enough. For cancer, it was too thin to say either way. It made no ruling on the heart, but calls it likely that nicotine adds somewhat to heart risk in people who smoke.

It says nicotine is the main thing in tobacco that hooks people, but nicotine medicines carry a low risk of that. In adults, even some who don't smoke, nicotine gave a small boost to thinking. Authors paid by tobacco firms reported almost only good effects on thinking.
cl_nic_smoke_or_nicotine.rate: One big US government report that sums up other studies and doesn't say how it found them. For nicotine on its own, it leans on animal studies and other products, not on people using nicotine alone.

cl_nic_smoke_nearby.short: Yes, two big US reports judge. It's linked to sudden infant death and asthma, and to 20 to 30% more lung cancer in adults who don't smoke.
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.but: These are the reports' judgments of other studies, so the figures are second-hand. And the later report builds on the earlier one.
how: In children, the 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence that others' smoke causes sudden infant death. The same went for chest and ear illness, wheeze, asthma at school age, weaker lungs and a small drop in birth weight. For early birth and some childhood cancers, the evidence was suggestive but not enough.

In adults who don't smoke, it found enough evidence for lung cancer and heart disease. Living with someone who smokes went with a 20 to 30% higher lung cancer risk, and heart disease risk was 25 to 30% higher.
The 2014 report added stroke, with a risk about 20 to 30% higher. It also found that smoke-free laws were followed by fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65.

The 2006 report says no level of secondhand smoke is risk-free. The parts we read give no figures for that, and by our reading it rests mostly on lab findings. The report expects less cancer risk than from smoking, since people breathe in far less of the cancer-causing chemicals.
cl_nic_smoke_nearby.rate: Two US government reports that sum up other studies, and the later builds on the earlier. We saw only their summaries, which is why the evidence counts as very limited here, not because the reports doubted the links.

cl_nic_cigars.short: It seems so. In big US studies, people who smoked only cigars died of mouth cancer 4 to 8 times as often as people who never smoked.
cl_nic_cigars.but: The studies began decades ago, mostly with white men who smoked big cigars. And the review didn't compare them with cigarettes.
how: A review by four staff at the US Food and Drug Administration looked at 16 long-running studies. They began between the 1940s and the 1980s. It compared people who smoked only cigars, never cigarettes or pipes, with people who never used tobacco.

Most figures come from two big American Cancer Society studies. Deaths from mouth cancer were about 4 to 8 times as common, from voice-box cancer about 10 times, and from lung cancer 2 to 5 times. Deaths from any cause were only slightly higher.

Risks mostly rose with more cigars a day and with inhaling the smoke. In the older study, even people who said they didn't inhale had more deaths from cancers of the mouth, gullet and voice box. The newer one had too few to be sure.

The review left out people who smoke cigarettes, so it can't show whether cigars are less or more harmful. Its authors still wrote that some cigar risks can be as high as cigarettes' or higher, which their tables can't show.
cl_nic_cigars.rate: The links are big and grew with more cigars, which helps. But the studies are old, mostly of white men, took little but age into account, and come through one review that didn't judge their quality.

cl_nic_snus.short: It may be. Among Swedish men who never smoked, those who used snus died at a rate about 28% higher than men who used no tobacco.
cl_nic_snus.but: This can't show snus caused it: men who used snus also drank more. And no source we read compared their overall death rate with people who smoke.
how: The biggest study pooled eight Swedish groups of men who had never smoked: 169,103 men, followed for about 17 years. Those who used snus died at a rate about 28% higher than men who used no tobacco, taking only age and weight into account.

Men who used snus drank more, and the main result didn't take drinking into account. The gap grew with the years men had used snus. One group of construction workers gave most of the deaths, and leaving it out made the gap bigger, not smaller.

An independent cancer review, which left out tobacco-industry work, estimated gullet cancer at about 55 in 100,000 men who used snus, against 16 who used no tobacco. Cancer deaths were about 2.4 in 100, against 2.1. Mouth and lung cancer showed no clear difference.

A review paid for by a snus maker found no clear harm; its author has long advised tobacco firms. A world cancer agency rates smokeless tobacco as a whole as causing cancer. It notes that Swedish snus is made to keep some cancer-causing chemicals low.
cl_nic_snus.rate: Studies of Swedish men, most from one group of construction workers, with snus use asked once. Men who used snus also drank more, and the sources disagree; one of them was paid for by a snus maker.

cl_nic_pouches.short: Nobody knows yet. No study has followed people who use them for more than 6 months, or looked at disease or death.
cl_nic_pouches.but: Most of what's known comes from lab tests and surveys, not from people's health. And the products differ a lot.
how: An independent German government lab tested 46 pouch products bought online in 2021, and 44 held nicotine. The amount varied a lot, and only 15 printed it in milligrams; 4 gave no sign of strength at all.

Traces of nitrosamines, cancer-causing chemicals from tobacco, turned up in 26 of the 44. Levels were far below those reported for snus. A pouch maker's own study found none above its test limit in two of its pouches.

In the US, about 2 in 100 middle and high school students used pouches in 2024, up from under 1 in 100 in 2021. Among adults it was under 1 in 100. Use was more common in males, younger people and people who smoked, vaped or used other tobacco.

Studies in people have lasted 6 months at most, and none looked at disease or death. In one small German study, as a review describes it, the two strongest pouches raised blood pressure and stiffened arteries about as much as a cigarette. That review's authors say pouches may be less harmful than tobacco but aren't risk-free.
cl_nic_pouches.rate: Mostly lab tests of products and surveys of who uses them, not studies of health. The studies in people were small and short, and several were paid for by pouch or tobacco makers.

cl_nic_nrt_forms.q: Patch, gum or both: which works best for quitting smoking?
cl_nic_nrt_forms.short: A patch plus gum or similar did a little better. In trials, about 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more, against 14 with one kind.
cl_nic_nrt_forms.but: The gain is small. And most people in these trials smoked about 20 or more cigarettes a day, so they say little about lighter smoking.
how: A Cochrane review pooled 16 trials with 12,169 people who wanted to quit. With a patch plus a quick form, like gum, a lozenge, an inhaler or a nose spray, 174 in 1,000 weren't smoking 6 months or more later, against 137 in 1,000 with one form. That's about 4 more in 100.

Both together did better than the patch alone and than a quick form alone, by about the same. The result held without the weakest trials, and a check found no sign of missing trials, though 16 is few for that check.
A quick form alone against the patch alone showed no clear difference: about 15 in 100 quit, against 16 in 100, in 8 trials. That doesn't rule out the patch doing somewhat better.

By our count, 9 of the 16 trials of both together had links to the products' makers, as funders, suppliers or employers. So did 6 of the 8 others. The review didn't check this, judging it mattered less when comparing ways of using the same products.
cl_nic_nrt_forms.rate: Strong: 16 trials comparing ways of using these products, with results that agree. One catch: over half had links to the products' makers, which the review didn't weigh.

cl_nic_nrt_harms.q: What side effects do nicotine patches and gum have?
cl_nic_nrt_harms.short: Irritation where they're used, like skin for patches and the mouth for gum. Chest pain or a pounding heart: 2.5 in 100, against 1.4 without.
cl_nic_nrt_harms.but: These come from trials lasting weeks to months. Serious problems were too rare to compare.
how: Trials reported most side effects too differently to add up, so a Cochrane review listed them by form. Patches can irritate the skin, usually mildly, in up to 54 in 100 people in one source it cites. Gum can bring hiccups, stomach upset and jaw pain; inhalers and sprays can irritate the mouth, throat or nose.

In the 15 trials that counted them, with 11,074 people, chest pain or a pounding heart came up in 2.5 in 100 people on nicotine replacement, against 1.4 in 100 on a dummy or nothing. That's about 1 more in 100.

A patch trial in people with heart disease didn't find more serious problems with the patch. In a later review, serious problems were too few to compare a patch plus a quick form with one form: 7 in all, across 5 trials.

More people stopped a quick form, like gum or a nose spray, because of side effects than stopped the patch: about 23 against 5 in 1,000, in 3 trials, which is very uncertain. In one trial, 3 in 100 stopped a nose spray, against about 1 in 100 the patch.
cl_nic_nrt_harms.rate: Trials where chance decided who got nicotine, but they recorded side effects in different ways, and only 15 of 136 counted chest pain or a pounding heart. Serious problems were too rare to judge.

cl_nic_vapes_stopping.q: Do vapes work better than patches or gum for quitting?
cl_nic_vapes_stopping.short: Yes, somewhat. In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a nicotine vape than with patches or gum.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping.but: In most trials that checked, more people kept using the vape than kept using patches or gum. And effects over years aren't known.
how: A Cochrane review, updated to January 2026, pooled 11 trials with 4,114 adults who smoked; most trials supplied the vape. If 6 in 100 quit with patches or gum, as the review assumes, about 10 in 100 would quit with a nicotine vape.
Against a vape without nicotine, a nicotine vape helped about 2 more in 100 quit, in 7 trials.

What people used afterwards is less certain. In the vape groups, more people were vaping without smoking and fewer were using neither. How long people kept vaping varied too much between trials to combine.
All trials were in adults, with regulated vapes. The results held without the one trial paid for by industry in each comparison, and without the weakest trials.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping.rate: Many trials where chance decided who got a vape. The review rates it high, but we rate it moderate: results varied between trials, and some small trials that found nothing may be unpublished.

cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.q: Does vaping actually help people quit smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.short: It may. In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more when given a vape than with counselling alone or nothing.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.but: People knew they got a vape, and the vape groups got more support too. So part of the gap may come from the extra help.
how: A Cochrane review, updated to January 2026, pooled 11 trials with 7,214 adults who smoked. If 5 in 100 quit with counselling alone or nothing, as the review assumes, about 9 in 100 would quit when given a nicotine vape.
The review rates this low: the trials couldn't hide who got a vape, and the vape groups had more support. The result held without the one trial paid for by a vape company.
Just advising people to vape, without giving them one, made no clear difference, in 2 trials with 2,652 people. All trials were in adults, and longer effects are unknown.
cl_nic_vapes_stopping_support.rate: Eleven trials where chance decided who got a vape, with results that agree. But people knew what they got, and the vape groups had more support, so the true gain may be smaller.

nicotine.statement: Quitting smoking after 55 is too late to make any difference.
nicotine.why: In a big US study, people who stopped at 55 to 64 gained roughly 4 years compared with people who kept smoking. That's a group average.

nicotine.statement: Quitting smoking by 40 wipes out all the extra risk of dying early.
nicotine.why: In a big US study, people who stopped around 40 still died at 1.2 times the rate of people who never smoked, against 3 times for those who kept smoking.

nicotine.statement: Nicotine gum and patches hook people as much as smoking does.
nicotine.why: A big US report says nicotine medicines carry a low risk of getting hooked. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

nicotine.statement: It's been proven that nicotine on its own causes cancer.
nicotine.why: A big US report found the evidence too thin to say either way. It says burned tobacco causes most of tobacco's harm.

nicotine.statement: Breathing other people's smoke has been linked to sudden infant death.
nicotine.why: A 2006 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence to call it a cause. That's the report's judgment of other studies.

nicotine.statement: After smoke-free laws came in, heart attacks fell in people under 65.
nicotine.why: A 2014 US Surgeon General's report found enough evidence for fewer heart attacks and similar events in people under 65. That's the report's judgment, second-hand.

nicotine.statement: If you don't inhale, cigars don't raise your risk of mouth cancer.
nicotine.why: In one big old US study, people who said they didn't inhale still died more often of mouth, gullet and voice-box cancer than people who never smoked. A second study had too few to be sure.

nicotine.statement: Swedish snus has been shown to raise the risk of mouth cancer.
nicotine.why: In an independent review, mouth cancer showed no clear difference between men who used snus and men who used no tobacco. A cancer agency's verdict covers all smokeless tobacco, not snus alone.

nicotine.statement: Snus has been linked to cancer of the gullet.
nicotine.why: An independent review estimated about 55 cases in 100,000 men who used snus, against 16 in men who used no tobacco. This can't show snus caused it.

nicotine.statement: Nicotine pouches have been shown to be safe in long-term studies.
nicotine.why: No study has followed people who use pouches for more than 6 months, or looked at disease or death.

nicotine.statement: The label on nicotine pouches always tells you how strong they are.
nicotine.why: In a German lab's test of 44 pouches bought in 2021, only 15 printed the nicotine in milligrams, and 4 gave no sign of strength at all.

nicotine.statement: A nicotine patch plus gum helped more people quit than one alone.
nicotine.why: In 16 trials, about 17 in 100 quit for 6 months or more with both, against 14 in 100 with one kind. The gain is small.

nicotine.statement: Skin problems from nicotine patches are rare.
nicotine.why: In one source a review cites, up to 54 in 100 people had skin irritation from patches, usually mild.

nicotine.statement: Chest pain or a pounding heart was no more common on nicotine patches and gum.
nicotine.why: In 15 trials, it came up in 2.5 in 100 people using them, against 1.4 in 100 on a dummy or nothing. Serious problems were too rare to compare.

nicotine.statement: In trials, nicotine vapes helped more people quit smoking than patches or gum.
nicotine.why: In 11 trials, about 4 more people in 100 quit for 6 months or more with a vape. More people kept vaping, and effects over years aren't known.

nicotine.statement: Simply advising people who smoke to vape helps them quit.
nicotine.why: In 2 trials, advice to vape without giving a vape made no clear difference. Being given a vape did better, but those trials couldn't hide who got one.
